exercises.objective: Compute forward kinematics for a small planar kinematic chain.
exercises.prompt: A 2-link planar arm has link lengths $L_1=L_2=1$, both joints revolute about $z$. Joint 1 is at the origin; joint 2's position is $p_1=(L_1\cos q_1,\,L_1\sin q_1)$; the end-effector position is $p_{\text{eff}} = p_1 + (L_2\cos(q_1+q_2),\,L_2\sin(q_1+q_2))$. At $q_1=0,\,q_2=\pi/2$, compute $p_{\text{eff}}$'s **second component** ($y$). Enter a decimal.

exercises.objective: Construct a Jacobian column geometrically from a joint's axis and location.
exercises.prompt: For the same arm at $q_1=0,q_2=\pi/2$ (so $p_1=(1,0,0)$, $p_{\text{eff}}=(1,1,0)$), both joint axes are $a_i=(0,0,1)$ (world $z$, since $q_1=0$ means no rotation has happened yet at joint 2 either). Using $J^{\text{pos}}_{\cdot 2}=a_2\times(p_{\text{eff}}-p_2)$ (with $p_2=p_1$, joint 2's location), compute the **first component** ($x$) of $J^{\text{pos}}_{\cdot 2}$. Enter a decimal.
hints: $a_2\times(p_{\text{eff}}-p_2) = (0,0,1)\times(0,1,0)$. Using the determinant/component formula for a cross product: $(0\cdot0-1\cdot1,\ 1\cdot0-0\cdot0,\ 0\cdot1-0\cdot0) = (-1,0,0)$.
First component: $-1$. (Independently verified against a finite-difference derivative of the forward-kinematics formula while authoring this module: matched exactly.)

exercises.objective: Apply the Gauss-Newton IK closed form numerically.
exercises.prompt: For the same arm, $q_0=(0,\pi/2)$, $\phi(q_0)=(1,1)$, $J=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ (rows $x,y$; columns joint 1, joint 2). Target $y^*=(1.2,1.2)$, $C=I$, $W=0.1I$. Using $\delta = (J^\top CJ+W)^{-1}J^\top C(y^*-\phi(q_0))$, compute $\delta_1$ (the first component). Enter a decimal to 3 decimal places.
hints: Solve $\begin{pmatrix}2.1&1\\1&1.1\end{pmatrix}\delta=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-0.2\end{pmatrix}$: determinant $=2.1(1.1)-1=1.31$. $\delta_1 = (0(1.1)-(-0.2)(1))/1.31 = 0.2/1.31 \approx 0.153$. (Independently verified with NumPy while authoring this module.)

exercises.objective: Explain Jacobian singularity and why regularization fixes the pseudo-inverse blowup.
exercises.prompt: Explain, geometrically, why a robot arm's Jacobian becomes singular when the arm is fully outstretched (at the boundary of its reachable workspace), and explain why using $J^\sharp=(J^\top CJ+W)^{-1}J^\top C$ with $W\succ0$ (rather than the naive pseudo-inverse $J^\top(JJ^\top)^{-1}$) avoids the resulting numerical blowup.
hints: At full stretch, every joint's rotation moves the end-effector in the same tangential direction (perpendicular to the fully-extended arm) — there's no combination of joint velocities that can move the end-effector directly outward/inward along the arm's own direction at that instant. This is exactly a rank deficiency: the columns of $J$ no longer span all $d$ output dimensions.

When $\text{rank}(J)<d$, $JJ^\top$ becomes singular (non-invertible), so the naive pseudo-inverse $J^\top(JJ^\top)^{-1}$ requires inverting a singular matrix, blowing up numerically (an IK step could request an 'infinite' joint velocity).

Adding $W\succ0$ inside $(J^\top CJ+W)^{-1}$ (or equivalently, per MATH-04's shift-invariance fact, shifting $J^\top CJ$'s eigenvalues up by at least $W$'s smallest eigenvalue) guarantees $J^\top CJ+W$ stays strictly positive definite and invertible even when $J^\top CJ$ alone is singular, exactly the same ridge-regression/Levenberg-Marquardt fix seen elsewhere in this course, here protecting IK from ever requesting an unbounded joint velocity near a singularity.
